topics.title: Two arrays combine elementwise
topics.body: Arithmetic between two same-shape arrays pairs position by position, so `a + b` is not concatenation and the result keeps the input shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)

topics.title: Indexing starts at zero
topics.body: The first element is index 0 and the last is -1, exactly like a Python list, so the same counting rules carry over before reshape changes anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Methods return plain results
topics.body: sum, min and max are methods on the array, so the answer arrives as a Python scalar you can print or compare without converting anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.sum(), a.max(), a.min())

topics.title: Convert back to a Python list
topics.body: tolist() turns an ndarray into nested Python lists, which is the right move when the receiver expects plain lists rather than array printing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Integers and floats carry different dtypes
topics.body: The dtype is inferred from the values you pass, so `np.array([1, 2])` is integer while `np.array([1.0, 2.0])` is float — one of them can hold 2.5 and the other cannot.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0, 2.0]).dtype)

debug.title: The array replaced the module name
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
np = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.arange(2))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.arange(2))
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'arange'

topics.title: len counts the first axis only
topics.body: len() reports the length of axis 0, not the number of elements, so for a (3, 4) array len is 3 while size is 12.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(len(a), a.size)

topics.title: Transpose swaps the shape
topics.body: Transposing reverses the axis order, so a (3, 4) array becomes (4, 3) and every operation that follows reads the new shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(a.T.shape)

topics.title: Mixed literals promote to float
topics.body: One float in the input is enough to make the whole array float64, because a single dtype has to hold every value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)

topics.title: A zero-dimensional array has no axes
topics.body: `np.array(7)` is a 0-d array: it has one value, ndim 0 and an empty shape tuple, which is how a scalar crosses into array code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
s = np.array(7)
print(s.ndim, s.shape)

topics.title: Bytes are shape times itemsize
topics.body: nbytes is size multiplied by itemsize, so a float32 array of six elements costs 24 bytes and a float64 one would cost 48.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.float32)
print(a.nbytes)

debug.title: shape used like a function
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a.shape(0))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a.shape[0])
debug.error: TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable

topics.title: zeros_like copies a shape
topics.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))

topics.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
topics.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))

topics.title: arange accepts a fractional step
topics.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))

topics.title: ones can take an integer dtype
topics.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))

topics.title: full repeats any value
topics.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))

debug.title: A float number of points
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 2.5))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 3))
debug.error: TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer

topics.title: astype truncates toward zero
topics.body: Casting float to int does not round: it drops the fractional part, so 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int))

topics.title: Text becomes a number with astype
topics.body: Numeric strings cast cleanly to int or float, which is exactly why one bad token in a loaded column raises instead of silently becoming zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(float))

topics.title: Division always yields floats
topics.body: True division produces float64 even when both operands are integers, so `int / int` never silently loses the remainder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2]) / 2).dtype)

topics.title: Numbers become booleans by truthiness
topics.body: Casting to bool keeps only whether a value is non-zero, so 0 becomes False and every other number becomes True.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([0, 1, 2]).astype(bool))

topics.title: Count with a boolean array
topics.body: Booleans add as 1 and 0, so sum() on a mask counts the matches without any branching code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.sum())

debug.title: One text value breaks the cast
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "x"]).astype(int))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(int))
debug.error: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'

topics.title: Index with a coordinate pair
topics.body: Two indices in one bracket address a single cell, row first then column, and the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[1, 2])

topics.title: One index drops a dimension
topics.body: Indexing a single row of a (2, 3) array returns shape (3,), because that axis is consumed by the integer index.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[0].shape)

topics.title: Select a whole column
topics.body: A colon keeps the row axis and the integer picks the column, so `a[:, 1]` is the second column of every row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: Fancy indexing picks rows
topics.body: An array of indices selects in exactly the order you give it, so repeats and reordering are allowed and the output grows to match the index list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[[0, 1, 0]])

topics.title: take works along an axis
topics.body: np.take does the same selection as fancy indexing but names the axis, which makes the intent readable in longer pipelines.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(np.take(a, [2, 0], axis=1))

debug.title: An index that is not an integer
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1.5])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1])
debug.error: IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices

topics.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

topics.title: Slice assignment writes through
topics.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Step in both dimensions
topics.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

topics.title: Copy breaks the view link
topics.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

topics.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
topics.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

debug.title: A row slice given the wrong width
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
a[0:2] = [1, 2]
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
a[0:2] = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
debug.error: ValueError: could not broadcast input array from shape (2,) into shape (2,3)

topics.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
topics.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

topics.title: newaxis makes a column
topics.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[:, np.newaxis].shape)

topics.title: stack adds a new axis
topics.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.stack([np.zeros(2), np.ones(2)]).shape)

topics.title: split cuts an array into pieces
topics.body: split divides an array into equal parts and returns a list, which is handy for batches or train/test cuts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.split(np.arange(4), 2))

topics.title: flatten always copies
topics.body: flatten returns a fresh 1-D array, so editing it never touches the source; ravel returns a view whenever the layout allows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 9
print(a[0])

debug.title: A reshape that cannot hold the elements
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(8).reshape(2, 3)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(8).reshape(2, 4)
debug.error: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 8 into shape (2,3)

topics.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
topics.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

topics.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
topics.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: clip limits every element
topics.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

topics.title: round, floor and ceil differ
topics.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

topics.title: sign tells you direction
topics.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

debug.title: sqrt called as an array method
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(a.sqrt())
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.sqrt(a))
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'sqrt'

topics.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: A column broadcasts down
topics.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

topics.title: Outer product uses two new axes
topics.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

topics.title: Comparison broadcasts too
topics.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

topics.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
topics.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

debug.title: A row vector where a column was needed
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2])
print(a + v)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2]).reshape(2, 1)
print(a + v)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (2,)

topics.title: median is not the mean
topics.body: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median, so reporting both is how you notice a skewed column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.median([1, 2, 100]), np.mean([1, 2, 100]))

topics.title: keepdims keeps a column
topics.body: keepdims=True leaves the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array without a reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: average can weight values
topics.body: np.average accepts weights, so a weighted mean is one call instead of a manual sum of products divided by a sum of weights.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 2], weights=[1, 3]))

topics.title: any and all answer yes/no
topics.body: On a boolean array, any asks whether at least one element is True and all asks whether every element is, each returning a single bool.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False])
print(m.any(), m.all())

topics.title: prod multiplies the elements
topics.body: prod folds with multiplication instead of addition, which is how compound growth and factorial-style products are computed in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.prod(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])))

debug.title: A string axis name
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis='row'))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=1))
debug.error: TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer

topics.title: Combine masks with & and |
topics.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

topics.title: Invert a mask with ~
topics.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

topics.title: Assign through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Count how many match
topics.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

topics.title: Filter rows by one column
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

debug.title: Two masks joined with and
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) and (a < 4)])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])
debug.error: ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()

topics.title: sort each row separately
topics.body: axis=1 sorts inside each row and leaves rows in place, while axis=0 would sort down each column instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [9, 7, 8]])
print(np.sort(a, axis=1))

topics.title: Reverse a sorted array for descending order
topics.body: sort only goes ascending, so descending order is a sort followed by a reverse slice — two views, no extra list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1])

topics.title: partition keeps only k small values in front
topics.body: partition is cheaper than a full sort when you only need the k smallest elements to be correct, which is enough for top-k work.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
part = np.partition([5, 1, 4, 2, 3], 2)
print(part[:3].sum(), part[3:].sum())

topics.title: lexsort orders by the last key first
topics.body: lexsort takes several keys and sorts by the last one primarily, which is how you order by two columns without building tuples.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['b', 'a', 'b', 'a'])
scores = np.array([2, 2, 1, 1])
order = np.lexsort((scores, names))
print(names[order], scores[order])

topics.title: argmax finds the best position
topics.body: argmax returns the index of the largest value, so you keep the label or row that produced the maximum instead of the maximum alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.argmax([3, 9, 5]))

debug.title: A reverse keyword that does not exist
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2], reverse=True))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1])
debug.error: TypeError: sort() got an unexpected keyword argument 'reverse'

topics.title: reshape usually returns a view
topics.body: When the memory is contiguous, reshape hands back a new shape over the same buffer, so shares_memory is True and writes travel both ways.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(np.shares_memory(a, b))

topics.title: base points at the source array
topics.body: A view keeps a reference to the array it came from in .base, which is the quickest way to prove two names share one buffer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1:].base is a)

topics.title: Transpose is a view with new strides
topics.body: Transposing changes only the strides, not the data, so a (2, 3) float64 array transposes to strides (8, 24) with the same bytes.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.strides)

topics.title: A reversed slice has negative strides
topics.body: A step of -1 stores a negative stride, which is why reversing is free: the array simply walks its memory backwards.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(4)[::-1].strides)

topics.title: copy owns its memory
topics.body: The OWNDATA flag tells you whether an array owns its buffer or borrows it, which is the truth behind the view/copy question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a.copy().flags['OWNDATA'])

debug.title: A flag name in the wrong case
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a.flags['own_data'])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a.flags['OWNDATA'])
debug.error: KeyError: 'own_data'

topics.title: integers draw inside a half-open range
topics.body: integers(low, high) returns values from low up to but excluding high, and the seeded generator makes the draw reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, 5))

topics.title: random floats sit between 0 and 1
topics.body: random returns floats in [0, 1), which you scale and shift into any interval you need.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(rng.random(3).round(3))

topics.title: the same seed gives the same numbers
topics.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce identical streams, which is the whole reason experiments are reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
b = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
print(np.allclose(a, b))

topics.title: size controls the shape of a draw
topics.body: Passing a tuple to size returns a multi-dimensional draw, so a batch of samples is one call instead of a loop of calls.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.normal(size=(2, 3)).shape)

topics.title: permutation shuffles a copy
topics.body: permutation returns a shuffled copy and leaves the input alone, so sorting the result recovers the original values exactly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
print(np.sort(rng.permutation(5)))

debug.title: Calling the old seed method on the new generator
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng()
rng.seed(0)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
debug.error: AttributeError: 'numpy.random._generator.Generator' object has no attribute 'seed'

topics.title: dot product of two vectors is a scalar
topics.body: The @ operator on two 1-D arrays sums the pairwise products, so the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a @ b)

topics.title: matrix times vector keeps the rows
topics.body: A (2, 2) matrix times a (2,) vector returns one value per row, so the output length is the number of rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(A @ v)

topics.title: solve then verify
topics.body: solve returns the x in Ax = b directly; checking A @ x against b is how you prove the answer instead of trusting it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([3., 5.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x, np.allclose(A @ x, b))

topics.title: norm measures length
topics.body: np.linalg.norm gives the Euclidean length by default, so a (3, 4) vector reports 5.0 and needs no manual square root.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linalg.norm([3, 4]))

topics.title: lstsq also fits inconsistent systems
topics.body: When the system has no exact solution, lstsq returns the least-squares answer so a tall, over-determined fit still works.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])

topics.title: skiprows ignores a header line
topics.body: loadtxt has no header concept, so skiprows=1 is how a CSV header is dropped before the numbers are parsed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_head.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('x,y\n1,2\n3,4\n')
print(np.loadtxt(p, delimiter=',', skiprows=1))

topics.title: genfromtxt fills missing values
topics.body: genfromtxt tolerates gaps and puts nan where a value is absent, which is exactly what loadtxt would refuse to parse.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_gap.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('1,2\n3,\n')
print(np.genfromtxt(p, delimiter=','))

topics.title: npz stores several arrays
topics.body: savez writes named arrays into one archive and load exposes them by name through .files, so a whole dataset travels as a single file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_bundle.npz')
np.savez(p, a=np.arange(2), b=np.ones(3))
d = np.load(p)
print(sorted(d.files), d['a'])

topics.title: memmap reads without loading everything
topics.body: memmap maps a binary file onto an array shape, so a very large matrix can be indexed while only the touched pages come from disk.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_raw.bin')
np.arange(10, dtype='float64').tofile(p)
m = np.memmap(p, dtype='float64', mode='r', shape=(2, 5))
print(m.shape, m[1, 0])

topics.title: savetxt writes formatted text
topics.body: savetxt needs an explicit fmt or it falls back to float formatting, so an integer table is written with fmt='%d' and a delimiter you choose.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_out.csv')
np.savetxt(p, np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), delimiter=',', fmt='%d')
print(open(p).read().strip())

topics.title: Fixed-width strings truncate
topics.body: A U2 dtype stores at most two characters per element, so longer text is cut on creation rather than at print time.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["abcd"], dtype="U2"))

topics.title: object dtype keeps Python objects
topics.body: dtype=object stores pointers to arbitrary Python values, which is flexible but loses the fast numeric paths that make arrays worthwhile.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, "x", None], dtype=object)
print(a.dtype, a[1])

topics.title: timedelta64 tells the gap
topics.body: Subtracting two datetime64 values returns a timedelta64, so date arithmetic reports an interval in the unit of the operands.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01'))

topics.title: Divide a timedelta to get a count
topics.body: Dividing a timedelta64 by a unit timedelta converts it to a plain number, which is how you get days, hours or seconds for analysis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01')
print(d / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

topics.title: Fields are read by name
topics.body: A structured array indexes its fields by name, so a price column is a plain array you can sum without unpacking the records.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5), (2, 3.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('price', 'f4')])
print(a['price'].sum())

topics.title: isnan builds the mask
topics.body: NaN never equals itself, so isnan is the only reliable way to locate missing values before you decide to drop or fill them.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan])
print(np.isnan(a))

topics.title: nanmean ignores missing values
topics.body: mean propagates one NaN to the answer while nanmean skips those elements and averages the rest, so the two numbers differ on dirty data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan, 3.])
print(np.mean(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: nan_to_num replaces NaN and infinity
topics.body: nan_to_num swaps non-finite values for finite defaults, which keeps a downstream model from receiving poisoning values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num(np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))

topics.title: allclose can treat NaN as equal
topics.body: By default two NaNs are not close, because allclose compares with ==; equal_nan=True is the switch that makes them match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan], equal_nan=True), np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan]))

topics.title: nanargmax skips NaN
topics.body: argmax can return the position of a NaN, while nanargmax ignores them and returns the position of the largest real value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nanargmax([1., np.nan, 3.]))

debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.isnan(np.array([1, 'a'])))
debug.fix:

print(np.isnan(np.array([1.0, np.nan])))

topics.title: einsum replaces a triple loop
topics.body: einsum writes the sum over indices in the subscript string, so a dot product, a trace or a batched contraction is one compiled call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3.)
print(np.einsum('i,i->', a, a))

topics.title: dot and @ agree
topics.body: np.dot and the @ operator compute the same matrix product, and proving it with allclose is a good habit before optimising either side.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.arange(4.).reshape(2, 2)
B = np.eye(2)
print(np.allclose(np.dot(A, B), A @ B))

topics.title: bincount counts integer categories
topics.body: bincount tallies non-negative integers in one pass, so labelled data is counted without a Python loop or a dictionary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])))

topics.title: vectorize wraps a Python function
topics.body: np.vectorize applies a scalar function elementwise for convenience, but it loops in Python underneath and is not a speed-up.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
f = np.vectorize(lambda x: x * x)
print(f(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: sum in chunks instead of one huge temporary
topics.body: Adding slice sums keeps peak memory small, because each chunk is released instead of materialising a full-size intermediate array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(a[i:i + 4].sum() for i in range(0, 10, 4)))

topics.title: Standardise each column
topics.body: Subtracting the column mean and dividing by the column standard deviation is broadcasting, and it is the step every model expects before training.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
print(Z.round(2))

topics.title: One-hot encode with eye
topics.body: Indexing an identity matrix with integer labels encodes a class vector into a matrix, no loop and no library needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
labels = np.array([0, 2, 1])
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int)[labels])

topics.title: Images are uint8 arrays
topics.body: An image is just a (height, width, channels) array of unsigned bytes, so brightness is an addition clipped back into 0-255.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.array([[0, 128], [255, 64]], dtype=np.uint8)
bright = np.clip(img.astype(int) + 40, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
print(bright)

topics.title: A moving average is a convolution
topics.body: np.convolve with a window of 1/n computes a moving average, which is the array-only way to smooth a series without pandas.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
print(np.convolve(v, np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid'))

topics.title: Round only for display
topics.body: Rounding is a presentation choice: keep the full float for computation, and round only when the number is about to be shown.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round(2.675, 2), np.round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))
